newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka says to add extra thermal power to grid.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka says to add extra thermal power to grid.

text.p: Sri Lanka's plans to add more than 150 megawatts of thermal power to the national grid by the end of this month should minimise the risk of drought-related power cuts in future, government officials said on Wednesday.

Officials at the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) said the state power utility plans to commission a 115-megawatt gas turbine and a 40-megawatt diesel plant before the end of the month, reducing Sri Lanka's dependence on hydropower to about 70 percent of its needs from the current 85 percent.
"Both these projects are onstream as planned. They should be adding power to the grid in the coming weeks," a CEB official told Reuters.
The 115-megawatt gas turbine plant at the CEB's Kelanitissa complex just outside Colombo would be operational within two weeks, an engineer with the project said.
"We are now conducting commissioning tests. We hope to gradually begin generating in the next two weeks," he said.
Power from the CEB's 40-megawatt diesel plant, located in the Colombo suburb of Sapugaskanda, will be added to the grid before the end of June, an official of that project said.

The plants are part of a crucial plan by the CEB to reduce the Indian Ocean island's current dependence on hydropower after a crippling drought last year forced the government to impose daily eight-hour power cuts.
Earlier this year, the government banned the use of air conditioners operating on power from the national grid and urged private sector businesses to use their own generators.

The restrictions were imposed after water levels in hydro reservoirs, which supply 85 percent of grid power, plunged to dangerously low levels with the failure of the northeast monsoon and the delayed onset of the intermonsoon showers.
Tropical Sri Lanka has two rainy seasons. The southwest monsoon, the most important for fuelling hydroelectric plants, usually starts around the third week of May.
A Meteorology Department official told Reuters the southwest monsoon was already delayed. "Conditions (for the monsoon) are weak. We're not expecting it to come even in one week's time."
CEB officials said hydropower reservoirs had 442 gigawatt hours, or 35 percent of storage capacity, as of Wednesday.

"We do expect the monsoons to break soon and bring enough water into the reservoirs," one official said. "But even if we get only marginal rains, with the new plants coming on stream, we should be able to manage."
Sri Lanka now has an installed capacity of 1,135 megawatts of hydropower and 250 megawatts of thermal power.
The CEB has said it plans to cut dependence on hydropower eventually to 57 percent by building more thermal power plants and buying electricity from private plants.
Among the new private plants are a 51-megawatt diesel plant funded by a consortium headed by KHD Great Britain, a unit of Germany's Kloeckner-Humboldt-Deutz AG.
Scheduled to be operational by August 1998, the plant is expected to add about 16 percent more power to the grid.
Japan's Mitsui Engineering & Shipbuilding Company Ltd last month signed a letter of intent to build and operate a 60-megawatt barge-mounted power plant.

Among the CEB's long-term plans to boost thermal power over hydro is a 300-megawatt coal-fired plant in the northwest. The utility also has plans two, 150-megawatt combined cycle plants on the outskirts of Colombo.
